The '''Ratel''' is a South African [[infantry fighting vehicle]]. It was the first wheeled infantry fighting vehicle to enter service worldwide<ref name="USMC">{{cite journal| last = Besch| first = Edwin| title = Infantry fighting Vehicles: Their Evolution and Significance| journal = [[Marine Corps Gazette]]| pages = 50–60| publisher = [[Marine Corps Association]]| location = [[Marine Corps Base Quantico]]| date = July 1983}}</ref> and was built on a modified [[MAN Truck & Bus|MAN]] truck chassis.<ref name=Harmse/> The Ratel was designed in response to a [[South African Army]] specification for a light armoured vehicle suited to the demands of rapid offensives, providing maximum firepower and strategic mobility to [[mechanised infantry]] units intended to operate across the vast distances of Southern Africa.<ref name=Harmse/> Primarily envisaged in SADF doctrine as a vehicle that could deliver mechanised infantry and supporting fire to tanks in conventional warfare, it was also anticipated that the Ratel could form the centrepiece for semi-independent battlegroups where logistics or politics precluded the use of tanks.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Botha |first=Willem |title=Ratel: Making of a Legend (Volumes 1 and 2) |last2=De Vries |first2=Maj Gen (Ret) Roland |last3=Ehlert |first3=Lt Col (Ret) Jan |last4=Haddad |first4=William |last5=Nel |first5=Col (Ret) Dr Johan ("Sarge") |last6=Savides |first6=Brig Gen (Ret) Tony |last7=Van Der Westhuizen |first7=Lt Col (Ret) Wessie |publisher=The Ratel Book Team |year=2020 |isbn=978-0-620-83635-7 |edition=Collector's Edition (Hardback) |location=Pretoria |pages=120–122; 143 (Vol 1) 92–101 (Vol 2)}}</ref> The Ratel was a simple, economical design which helped reduce the significant logistical commitment necessary to keep heavier combat vehicles operational in undeveloped regions.<ref name=Harmse/> It was generally regarded as an influential concept<ref name=SurviveRide/> which incorporated a number of novel features, such as a mine-protected hull and a 20&nbsp;mm autocannon fitted with what was then a unique twin-linked ammunition feed, allowing turret gunners to rapidly swap between ammunition types during combat.<ref name=Harmse/>

The first Ratel prototype appeared in March 1972,<ref name=Mobility/> and serial production commenced in 1976.<ref name=SurviveRide/> Rights to the original prototype were also sold to [[Belgium]], which produced an amphibious derivative known as the [[SIBMAS]].<ref name="Landgren">{{cite book| first = Signe| last = Landgren| title = Embargo Disimplemented: South Africa's Military Industry| year = 1989| edition = 1989| pages = [https://archive.org/details/embargodisimplem0000land/page/83 83]–85| publisher = Oxford University Press| isbn = 978-0-19-829127-5| url = https://archive.org/details/embargodisimplem0000land| url-access = registration}}</ref> The Ratel was produced in three distinct marks<ref name=SurviveRide/> between 1976 and 1987, when production ceased.<ref name="Evolution"/> All three marks were modified for a number of diverse battlefield roles.<ref name=SurviveRide/> Specialised variants of the Ratel carried mortars, anti-tank guided missiles, or a turret-mounted 90&nbsp;mm rifled gun.<ref name=SurviveRide/>

== Development history ==
During the 1950s, the [[South African Defence Force]] (SADF) had been primarily organised to operate alongside the [[British Armed Forces]] in the event of a military crisis affecting the [[British Empire]]'s African or Middle Eastern dependencies.<ref name=Harmse/><ref name=Berridge>{{cite book|last=Berridge|first=G.R.|title=South Africa, the Colonial Powers and African Defence: The Rise and Fall of the White Entente, 1948–60|date=1992|pages=1–16, 163–164|publisher=Palgrave Books|location=Basingstoke|isbn=978-0333563519}}</ref> This reflected South Africa's longstanding defence ties to the [[United Kingdom]] and the other member states in the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].<ref name=Berridge/> As a result of its strategic priorities, the SADF adopted equipment which was either British in origin or otherwise compatible with Commonwealth doctrine.<ref name=Harmse/> South African infantry units were equipped primarily with [[Alvis Saracen]] armoured personnel carriers.<ref name=Harmse/> This reflected traditional British infantry doctrine, which placed a disproportionate emphasis on dismounted infantry; the role of armoured vehicles like the Saracen was to function as general transporters conveying infantrymen to a battlefield.<ref name="USMC"/> Afterwards, the infantry was expected to disembark and fight on foot rather than remaining mounted.<ref name="USMC"/>

The deterioration of relations between South Africa and the United Kingdom in the wake of the [[Sharpeville Massacre]] marked a shift in the SADF's doctrine and strategic priorities.<ref name=Harmse/> The SADF became more focused on the threat of domestic insurgency or limited bush conflicts rather than a major conventional war overseas.<ref name=Harmse/> Additionally, the British government's refusal to supply the SADF with new armoured vehicles forced it to turn to alternative suppliers, namely [[France]] and [[West Germany]].<ref name=Nigeria>{{cite book|last=Wayas|first=Joseph|title=Nigeria's Leadership Role in Africa|date=1979|page=55|publisher=Macmillan|location=Basingstoke|isbn=978-0333262955}}</ref> Both nations cooperated closely with South African firms like [[Sandock-Austral]] to set up the country's first armoured vehicle factory at [[Boksburg]].<ref name="Landgren"/><ref name=Nigeria/> West Germany was especially instrumental in the transfer of defence technology; in exchange it received a higher import quota for its automotive products to South Africa.<ref name="Landgren"/> One result was that German companies came to dominate several sectors of the South African civilian and military vehicle market, including achieving a virtual monopoly on the sale of trucks to the SADF.<ref name="Landgren"/> Much of this business was conducted through local subsidiaries such as Springfield-Büssing SA, an [[East Rand]] company which was the franchise holder for all Büssing products in South Africa.<ref name="SADigest">{{cite journal|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aa9g71TD07YC|date=1971|title= Bus Plant for Natal|journal=South African Digest|publisher=South African Information Service|page=6}}</ref> Springfield-Büssing assembled its vehicles with locally manufactured bodies and engine and chassis components imported from its German parent firm.<ref name="SADigest"/>

In 1968, the SADF began formulating a new mobile warfare doctrine which centered around the independent deployment of mechanised infantry to defend the vast borders of [[South West Africa]] ([[Namibia]]), which were deemed vulnerable to the threat of insurgency and external infiltration.<ref name=Mobility/> Mechanised infantry mounted in their own [[infantry fighting vehicle]]s (IFVs) could arrive sooner at contact points, with greater firepower to engage and destroy the enemy where contact was made, as well as greater protection and convenience for troops.<ref name=Mobility/> During wargaming exercises designed to simulate a foreign invasion of South West Africa, the SADF found none of its preexisting armoured vehicles suitable to fill this role, so development of a new dedicated IFV was undertaken.<ref name=Mobility/> Any South African IFV had to be a simple, economical design which helped ease the significant logistical commitment to maintain armoured vehicles in border regions otherwise lacking in advanced support or transport infrastructure.<ref name=Harmse/> Excessive track wear inflicted by the abrasive, sandy terrain of the South West African border prompted South African officials to specify a wheeled vehicle.<ref name=Harmse/> Wheeled IFVs were also favoured because they possessed a much greater operating range than tracked vehicles, and did not require the use of transporters on South West Africa's limited road and rail network.<ref name=Harmse/> This marked a significant departure from Soviet and Western IFV doctrine, which had rejected wheeled IFVs for their inferior cross-country capability and weight-carrying capacity, as well as the vulnerable nature of their tyres to small arms fire and artillery fragments.<ref name="USMC"/> However, improvements in power train, suspension, and run-flat tyre technology during the late 1960s helped make the concept of wheeled IFVs more viable.<ref name="USMC"/> The SADF initially had no other requirements other than a chassis and hull combination capable of supporting a two-man turret.<ref name=Mobility/>

Springfield-Büssing proposed a six-wheeled IFV built on a modified MAN truck chassis;<ref name=Harmse/> the first prototype appeared as the ''Springfield-Büssing Buffel'' in March 1972.<ref name=Mobility/> After the SADF had evaluated and rejected a number of other designs, including the [[Thyssen Henschel UR-416]], [[Berliet VXB-170]], [[Panhard M3]], and the [[EE-11 Urutu]], the Springfield-Büssing prototype was accepted for service as the ''Ratel''.<ref name=Mobility/> Production was undertaken by Sandock-Austral, which produced the vehicle hulls at its shipyard in Durban before having them transported by rail to its Boksburg facility for integration with the chassis and drive train.<ref name=Mobility/> Each Ratel was powered by a Büssing D 3256 six-cylinder diesel engine fitted in a compartment at the left rear of its hull with access panels in the roof for ease of maintenance; it could be changed by two technicians with a crane in thirty minutes.<ref name=SurviveRide/> It was armed with a 20&nbsp;mm autocannon, which was standard armament for most Western IFVs at the time and suitable for engaging low-flying aircraft, light armour, and dismounted personnel.<ref name="USMC"/> The SADF had selected the [[Hispano-Suiza HS.820]] for the Ratel's primary armament due to its prior success during trials with [[Eland Mk7|Eland]] armoured cars; however, at the time of production this was superseded by a variant of the [[20 mm modèle F2 gun|Modèle F2]] produced under licence as the [[Denel Land Systems GI-2|Denel GI-2]].<ref name=SurviveRide/>

The Ratel was first tested in combat during [[Operation Reindeer]], a major South African raid on [[People's Liberation Army of Namibia]] (PLAN) insurgents based out of neighbouring [[Angola]].<ref name="Borderstrike">{{cite book | first = Willem | last = Steenkamp| title = Borderstrike! South Africa Into Angola 1975-1980| year = 2006|edition= 2006|pages= 43, 96, 134–142, 190 | publisher = Just Done Productions| isbn= 1-920169-00-8}}</ref> For the purposes of Operation Reindeer, the SADF experimented with an integrated combat team consisting of mechanised infantry mounted in the new Ratels, backed by attached Eland armoured cars.<ref name="McGill">{{cite journal| title=The Cassinga Raid| first=Edward| last=McGill Alexander| publisher=[[UNISA]]| format=[[PDF]]| date=July 2003| url=http://uir.unisa.ac.za/bitstream/handle/10500/1475/00dissertation.pdf?sequence=4| access-date=22 February 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141124152157/http://uir.unisa.ac.za/bitstream/handle/10500/1475/00dissertation.pdf?sequence=4| archive-date=24 November 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> This caused a number of delays and complications, since the four-wheeled Elands lacked sufficient mobility to keep pace with the Ratels and had to be frequently towed out of thick sand or mud.<ref name="Eagles">{{cite book | first = Jan | last = Breytenbach| title = Eagle strike!: the controversial airborne assault on Cassinga| date = 19 December 2014|edition= 2008|page= 193 | publisher = Manie Publishing| isbn= 978-1909982307}}</ref> Operation Reindeer was also complicated by the fact that the Elands utilised petrol engines, which necessitated a separate logistics tail from that of the diesel-powered Ratels.<ref name="Lessons">{{cite web|title=The Lessons of the Border War|last1=Scholtz|first1=Leopold|url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/smsajms/article/viewFile/89172/78726|location=Stellenbosch
|publisher=Military Science Department, Stellenbosch University|date=2012|access-date=24 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150128103422/http://www.ajol.info/index.php/smsajms/article/viewFile/89172/78726|archive-date=28 January 2015}}</ref>

[[File:Ratel90mm2.PNG|thumb|240px|Ratel Mk II, identifiable by its exposed headlamps and the armoured cover plates over its wheel hubs.<ref name="Sandstone1"/>]]

Although PLAN possessed little conventional warfare capabilities, it was frequently backed by its allies in the [[Cuba]]n and Angolan armed forces, which were skilled at constructing well-fortified defensive positions and had access to heavy armour.<ref name="Warwick">{{cite journal |last=Warwick |first=Rodney |date=2012|title=Operation Savannah: A Measure of SADF Decline, Resourcefulness and Modernisation|journal=Scientia Militaria|volume=40| issue =  3|pages=354–397}}</ref> The addition of attached Eland squadrons to mechanised infantry units was considered necessary because they carried 60&nbsp;mm breech-loading mortars or large 90&nbsp;mm guns, which were more useful than the Ratel's 20&nbsp;mm autocannon for engaging fixed fortifications, dug-in troops, and enemy armour as needed.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> However, the Eland's shortcomings in terms of mobility and logistics prompted the SADF to replace it with new variants of the Ratel carrying the same armament.<ref name=Tartan>{{cite book|last=Mitchell|first=James|title=Tartan on the veld: the Transvaal Scottish, 1950−1993|date=1994|page=521|publisher=Transvaal Scottish Regimental Council & Thorold's Africana Books|location=Johannesburg|isbn=978-0620178426}}</ref> The ''Ratel-90'' fire support vehicle utilised an Eland turret with a 90&nbsp;mm rifled cannon firing conventional [[Shell (projectile)#HE-Frag|high explosive]] and [[High-explosive anti-tank warhead|high explosive anti-tank]] shells, while the ''Ratel-60'' mortar carrier was fitted with an Eland turret mounting a 60&nbsp;mm mortar.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> A third variant, the ''Ratel Command'', was introduced shortly thereafter and functioned as a mobile command post.<ref name=Williams>{{cite book|last=Williams|first=David|title=On the Border: The White South African Military Experience, 1965-1990|date=2008|pages=322–342|publisher=Tafelberg Publishers|location=Cape Town|isbn=978-0624044697}}</ref> The Ratel Command was fitted with additional radio equipment, a public address system, and map tables; it carried a 12.7&nbsp;mm machine gun as its main armament.<ref name=Williams/> The ''Ratel-81'' was a turretless variant with an 81&nbsp;mm mortar installed in the passenger compartment.<ref name=SurviveRide/> The ''Ratel ZT3'' was the final variant to be produced and was armed with a bank of [[ZT3 Ingwe]] [[anti-tank guided missile]]s.<ref name=Williams/>

In 1979, Sandock-Austral introduced the Ratel Mk II, which included a number of functional modifications designed to optimise the vehicle for southern African conditions and improve mechanical reliability.<ref name=SurviveRide/> In 1985, the Ratel Mk II was superseded by the Ratel Mk III, which incorporated a new cooling system and an automatic cocking mechanism for the 20&nbsp;mm autocannon.<ref name=SurviveRide/> Production ceased in 1987,<ref name=SurviveRide/> at which point 1,381 Ratels had been manufactured.<ref name="Sandstone1"/>

== Service history ==
At the time of the Ratel's introduction, South African military officials were attempting to bring combined arms integration to the lowest tactical level, using brigade or even battalion-sized units as the standard all-arms unit rather than divisions.<ref name="Lessons"/> In these theoretical combat battle groups, armoured squadrons and mechanised infantry, transported in Ratels, would be integrated at the company level, giving them sufficient flexibility to operate in concert.<ref name="Lessons"/> The SADF's first integrated battle group was Combat Group Juliet, which was envisaged as a conventional strike unit to be activated for raids on guerrilla sanctuaries and infiltration routes along the borders of South West Africa and neighbouring Angola.<ref name="Lessons"/> Combat Group Juliet consisted of two companies of mechanised infantry and a squadron of Eland armoured cars.<ref name="Lessons"/> Later combat groups replaced the Eland squadron with Ratel-90s, which essentially functioned in the same role.<ref name="Lessons"/>

Ratels formed the mainstay of the SADF's ''ad hoc'' battle groups for most of the [[South African Border War]]. As the Ratel and most of the SADF's other combat vehicles were lightly armoured, South African mechanised doctrine came to revolve around such tactics as rapid movement, striking from the flank, and confusing the enemy with continuous manoeuvring.<ref name="Scholtz">{{cite book|last=Scholtz|first=Leopold|title=The SADF in the Border War 1966-1989|year=2013|pages=41–46, 295, 379|publisher=Tafelberg|location=Cape Town|isbn=978-0-624-05410-8}}</ref> In this regard the SADF differed greatly from Western IFV doctrine–which confined the IFV's role to assisting the forward momentum of tanks–as well as Soviet IFV doctrine, which dictated that IFVs must occupy and hold terrain as needed.<ref name="Coffey">{{cite web|title=Doctrinal Orphan or Active Partner? A History of US Mechanized Infantry Doctrine|last=Coffey|first=Rod|url=http://www.dtic.mil/get-tr-doc/pdf?AD=ADA384122|location=[[Fort Leavenworth]]|publisher=[[United States Army Command and General Staff College]]|year=2000|access-date=17 February 2018}}{{dead link|date=June 2022|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Although capable of operating independently, Ratel-based battle groups were not expected to occupy and hold static positions; their primary task was to outmanoeuvre an enemy unit<ref name="Devries">{{cite journal |last=De Vries |first=Roland |date=2012|title=The Influence of the Ratel Infantry Fighting Vehicle on Mobile Warfare in Southern Africa|journal=Scientia Militaria|volume=43| issue =  2|pages=174–184}}</ref> before destroying it with a concentrated fire and movement tactic known as a ''firebelt action''.<ref name="RDV">{{Cite web |url=http://www.warinangola.com/portals/31/SOME%20REMININISCENSES%20ON%20THE%20OPERATIONS%20CONDUCTED%20BY%20COMBAT%20TEAM%203a.pdf |title=Some remininiscenses on the operations conducted by Combat Team 3 |access-date=2018-03-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304201356/http://www.warinangola.com/portals/31/SOME%20REMININISCENSES%20ON%20THE%20OPERATIONS%20CONDUCTED%20BY%20COMBAT%20TEAM%203a.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-04 |url-status=live }}</ref> This doctrine was suited for the wide, densely wooded expanses of southern Angola which enabled the South African forces to carry out evasive manoeuvres and strike quickly from unexpected directions without being prematurely detected.<ref name="Devries"/> Manoeuvre-oriented warfare depended on the Ratel's speed and mobility, which were used to maximum effect to compensate for its relatively light armour.<ref name=Harmse/>

A notable feature of the South African Border War was a cyclical pattern of increasing cross-border infiltration and raids by PLAN guerrillas, primarily from Angola, during the annual rainy season.<ref name="Vlamgat">{{cite book|last=Lord|first=Dick|title=Vlamgat: The Story of the Mirage F1 in the South African Air Force|year=2008|publisher=30° South Publishers|location=Johannesburg|isbn=978-1-920143-36-7|pages=83, 116, 149–152}}</ref> The SADF's Ratels and other wheeled combat vehicles were hampered by thick mud, and the increased foliage cover provided PLAN with concealment from patrols.<ref name="Vlamgat"/> The rainy season in South West Africa and southern Angola lasted from February to April.<ref name="Vlamgat"/> At the end of April or early May, when the heaviest rains ceased, South African mechanised battle groups launched retaliatory raids to capture or kill the insurgents in their external sanctuaries.<ref name="Vlamgat"/> While carrying out an attack, Ratels interspersed into arrowhead-shaped formations, with a platoon of Ratel-20s and a troop of Ratel-90s on each flank, the command Ratels located in the centre, and the remaining Ratels following in reserve.<ref name="Holt">{{cite book|title=At Thy Call We Did Not Falter|last=Holt|first=Clive|location=Cape Town|publisher=Zebra Press|year=2008|orig-year=2005|isbn=978-1770071179|pages=67–73}}</ref><ref name=Heitman2>{{cite book|last=Heitman|first=Helmoed-Romer|title=War in Angola: The Final South African Phase|date=1990|pages=57–61|publisher=Ashanti Publishing|location=Benoni|isbn=978-0620143707}}</ref> If the mechanised battle group was integrated with tanks&mdash;as during [[Operation Hooper]] and [[Operation Packer]]&mdash;the tanks spearheaded the formation to engage hostile armour, while the Ratel-20s and Ratel-90s followed closely on the flanks to suppress any accompanying infantry.<ref name="Holt"/> Ratel-81s, if present, occupied a place in the centre of the formation, directly behind the command Ratels.<ref name="Holt"/>

One of the primary threats to the Ratels were hidden bunkers and the maze of trench complexes constructed around PLAN and Angolan military camps.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> It was not uncommon for a Ratel crew to unwittingly drive atop an insurgent bunker, which collapsed under the weight of their vehicle and rendered it immobile.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> More frequently, Ratels were surrounded and cut off by PLAN defenders after bogging down in trenches.<ref name="Nortje">{{cite book|title=32 Battalion: The Inside Story of South Africa's Elite Fighting Unit|last=Nortje|first=Piet|location=New York|publisher=Zebra Press|year=2003|isbn=1-868729-141|page=88}}</ref> This necessitated their being towed out with recovery vehicles or other Ratels, often under heavy fire.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> PLAN training camps were defended by a number of [[ZU-23-2]] anti-aircraft guns, and these were used in the ground support role with deadly results for immobilised Ratel crews.<ref name=Harmse/>

During the early 1980s, PLAN carefully re-sited its training camps near Angolan military installations so it could take advantage of the security provided by the attached Angolan armoured and mechanised brigades.<ref name=Dale>{{cite book|last=Dale|first=Richard|title=The Namibian War of Independence, 1966-1989: Diplomatic, Economic and Military Campaigns|date=2014|pages=74–87, 93–95|publisher=McFarland & Company, Incorporated Publishers|location=Jefferson|isbn=978-0786496594}}</ref> This gave PLAN ready access to the logistical and communications infrastructure of its local allies and increased the risk to SADF raids targeting those camps exponentially.<ref name="George">{{cite book|title=The Cuban intervention in Angola |last=George|first=Edward|location=New York|publisher=Frank Cass Publishers|year=2005|isbn=978-0415647106|pages=75–77, 97–99}}</ref> The SADF remained conscious of this fact and established a number of improvised anti-tank platoons composed of Ratel-90s to engage Angolan armour if necessary.<ref name="61Protea">{{cite web|title=Operation Protea|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://www.61mech.org.za/operations/operation-protea|location=Modderfontein
|publisher=61 Mechanised Battalion Group Veterans' Association|date=2009|access-date=20 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105231630/http://www.61mech.org.za/operations/operation-protea|archive-date=5 November 2016}}</ref> During [[Operation Protea]] and [[Operation Askari]], Ratel-90s were to face Angolan [[T-34|T-34-85]], [[PT-76]], and [[T-54/55]] tanks, with mixed results.<ref name=Steenkamp2>{{cite book|last=Steenkamp|first=Willem|title=South Africa's Border War, 1966-1989|date=1989|page=99|publisher=Ashanti Publishing|location=Benoni|isbn= 978-0620139670}}</ref> While the Ratel-90s were for the most part adequate in countering Angola's largely obsolete and second-line Soviet tanks, they remained hindered by mediocre standoff ranges, inferior fire control, and a lack of stabilised main armament.<ref name="Grove">{{cite web|title=Ratel teen tenk en|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->
|url=http://www.samagte.co.za/weermag/hc/grove.html|url-status=dead|location=Port Elizabeth|publisher=International Veterans' Association/South African Forces Club|date=2011
|access-date=20 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120728040847/http://www.samagte.co.za/weermag/hc/grove.html|archive-date=28 July 2012}}</ref> Ratel crews often had to manoeuvre behind the tanks and fire on them from the rear to destroy them.<ref name="Nortje"/> This required intense coordination between the vehicle commanders, who directed each other by radio until they were in a position to concentrate volleys on a tank's exposed side or rear.<ref name=Harmse/> As the Angolan tank crews were in no position to out-manoeuvre the Ratels, they prioritised mobility kills.<ref name="Holt"/> A common tactic was to fire a round beneath the Ratel, destroying the differentials on its axles and rendering it immobile.<ref name="Holt"/> This stripped the Ratel of its most crucial advantage and made it an easy target for the other tanks.<ref name="Holt"/>
[[File:Sudan Envoy - Children with UN Tank.jpg|thumb|left|250px|SANDF troops and a Ratel attached to [[United Nations–African Union Mission in Darfur|UNAMID]] in [[Darfur]], 2009.]]
In the wake of Operation Askari, South African field commanders began complaining that Ratel-90s were being expected to fulfill the role of light tanks rather than serving in their intended role of infantry support.<ref name="Lessons"/> This was a violation of SADF mechanised and armoured doctrine.<ref name="Lessons"/> Consequently, the SADF introduced the Ratel ZT3 [[anti-tank missile carrier]], a Ratel variant designed as a dedicated tank destroyer, in 1987.<ref name=SurviveRide/> It was first deployed with marked success against Angolan T-54s during [[Operation Moduler]].<ref name=SurviveRide/> The Ratel ZT3 also saw limited action against Cuban T-55s during [[Operation Excite/Hilti]].<ref name="Scholtz"/>

The cessation of hostilities with Angola in 1989 and the amalgamation of the SADF into the new [[South African National Defence Force]] (SANDF) in 1995 ushered in consistent budget cuts to defence spending, resulting in a reduction of personnel and equipment.<ref name=DoD1998>{{cite web|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://www.dod.mil.za/documents/defencereview/defence%20review1998.pdf |title=South African Defence Review 1998 |publisher=South African Department of Defence |date=2006-09-26|access-date=2016-10-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160528115331/http://www.dod.mil.za/documents/defencereview/defence%20review1998.pdf |archive-date=May 28, 2016 }}</ref> At least 354 Ratels were declared surplus to requirements and sold beginning in 2005.<ref name=Surplus>{{cite web|url=http://www.news24.com/SouthAfrica/News/SANDF-gets-rid-of-surplus-20051004 |title=SANDF gets rid of surplus |publisher=South African Associated Press |date=2005-10-04 |access-date=2014-07-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150128102708/http://www.news24.com/SouthAfrica/News/SANDF-gets-rid-of-surplus-20051004 |archive-date=January 28, 2015 }}</ref> Much of the remaining Ratels have been handicapped by the SANDF's limited maintenance budget and inadequate numbers of trained maintenance personnel.<ref name="IISS2016"/> 

The Ratel was intended to be at least partly superseded in SANDF service by a new eight-wheeled infantry fighting vehicle, the [[Badger IFV]].<ref name="IISS2016"/> Work on this project was suspended in 2024 without any being delivered. The South African military is considering options to extend the service of the remaining Ratels following the deferment of the Badger project.<ref name="Hoefyster deferred">{{cite news |last1=Teixeira |first1=Ricardo |title=Project Hoefyster 'deferred' |url=https://www.defenceweb.co.za/featured/project-hoefyster-deferred/ |access-date=1 December 2024 |work=defenceWeb |date=27 November 2024 |language=en-ZA}}</ref>

=== Foreign service ===
After 1977, the domestic South African arms industry was driven by the economic realities of a universal [[arms embargo]] imposed on the SADF as a result of [[United Nations Security Council Resolution 418]].<ref name=Ohlson>{{cite book|last=Ohlson|first=Thomas|editor1-last=Zartman|editor1-first=William|editor2-last=Deng|editor2-first=Francis|title=Conflict Resolution in Africa|date=1991|pages=[https://archive.org/details/conflictresoluti0000unse/page/250 250]–252|publisher=The Brooking Institution|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=9780815717980|url=https://archive.org/details/conflictresoluti0000unse|url-access=registration}}</ref> The embargo deprived the SADF of many new weapons systems available to other major arms importers, curtailed its attempts to obtain defence technology on the open market, and raised the cost of obtaining spare parts and components for its preexisting equipment.<ref name=Ohlson/> While South Africa was able to partly compensate by developing its local arms industry, the SADF's requirements were too small to make the manufacture of a wide range of armaments economically profitable.<ref name=Ohlson/> Defence contractors were compelled to tool up for uneconomical and short production runs of sophisticated hardware, including military vehicles.<ref name=Ohlson/> Furthermore, the domestic manufacture of obsolete equipment items had to be sustained long after their basic technology had become quite dated, simply because no alternatives were available.<ref name="Landgren"/> These unprofitable practices threatened to result in stagnation for the defence sector; firms like Sandock-Austral looked for new ways to gain badly needed funds for future [[research and development]] efforts and counter their own rapidly rising production costs.<ref name=Ohlson/> In the early 1980s, South Africa's defence contractors turned to export orders to help create the economy of scale necessary to keep their operations viable.<ref name=Ohlson/> They embarked on a massive international marketing drive which included extensive advertising campaigns and exhibits at arms fairs.<ref name=Ohlson/> As a result, public information on vehicles like the Ratel became more readily available in connection with their manufacturers' marketing efforts.<ref name="Roherty">{{cite book|title=State Security in South Africa: Civil-military Relations Under P.W. Botha|last=Roherty|first=James Michael|location=New York|publisher=ME Sharpe Publishers|year=1992|isbn=978-0873328777|pages=112–115}}</ref>

The [[Royal Moroccan Army]] became the first prospective client to show an interest in the Ratel; it was then purchasing arms from a vast array of sources for use in the [[Western Sahara War]].<ref name="Sahara">{{cite book | last = Michael Brzoska| title = Arms and Warfare: Escalation, De-escalation, and Negotiation | date = July 2006 |edition= 1994|page=172 | publisher = University of South Carolina Press| isbn= 978-1422352960}}</ref> This was pursued as part of a massive re-armament programme being funded through generous military subsidies from [[Saudi Arabia]].<ref name="Sahara"/> Morocco initially made contact with Sandock-Austral after soliciting a French firm, [[Panhard]], for new [[Panhard AML|AML]] armoured cars.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> As Panhard was closing its AML production line, it declined the order but referred the Moroccan government to South Africa, where Sandock-Austral was still producing an AML derivative under licence as the Eland.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> Though extensively modified, the Eland was still familiar to Moroccan crews and maintenance personnel who had been trained by French instructors on the AML.<ref name=Challenge>{{cite book|last=Venter|first=Al J.|title=Challenge: Southern Africa within the African Revolutionary Context|date=1989|page=483|publisher=Ashanti Publishing|location=Rivonia|isbn=978-0620121903}}</ref> Morocco received the first Elands in 1976<ref name="Fuel">{{cite book | last = Leo Kamil| title = Fueling the Fire: U.S. Policy & the Western Sahara Conflict | year = 1987 |edition= 1987|page=62 | publisher = Red Sea Press| isbn= 978-0932415233}}</ref> and obligingly placed orders for more vehicles, including a few dozen Ratels, from Sandock-Austral.<ref name="Sahara"/> These were delivered between 1978 and 1980.<ref name="Sahara"/> The Royal Moroccan Army ordered another 80 Ratels in 1979, which were delivered between 1980 and 1981.<ref name=Lambrechts>{{cite book|last=Lambrechts|first=Kato|title=Paris, Pretoria and the African Continent: The International Relations of States and Societies in Transition|date=1996|page=155|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|location=Basingstoke|isbn=978-0333651339}}</ref> They were deployed in counter-insurgency operations against the [[Polisario Front]], which captured several Ratel-20s and pressed them into service.<ref name=Maghreb>{{cite book|last=Cordesman|first=Anthony|title=A Tragedy of Arms: Military and Security Developments in the Maghreb|date=2001|pages=62, 94|publisher=Praeger Books|location=Westport|isbn=978-0275969363}}</ref><ref name=Cordesman2016>{{cite book|last=Cordesman|first=Anthony|title=After The Storm: The Changing Military Balance in the Middle East|date=October 2016|pages=107–112|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing|location=London|isbn=978-1-4742-9256-6}}</ref> In 2016, Morocco was still operating 30 Ratel-20s and 30 Ratel-90s.<ref name="IISS2016">{{cite book|last=International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS)|title=The Military Balance 2016|year=2016|publisher=IISS|location=London|isbn=978-1857438352}}</ref> All of these were the Ratel Mk III variant.<ref name="IISS2016"/>

[[File:Royal Tank Museum 157.jpg|thumb|250px|Jordanian Ratel-20 in the [[Royal Tank Museum]], [[Amman]].]]

Sandock-Austral's attempts to secure new export customers for the Ratel were somewhat curtailed by the passage of [[United Nations Security Council Resolution 558]], which amended the arms embargo to prohibit all member states from importing South African military equipment.<ref name=Ohlson/> At the time production of the Ratel ceased in 1987, no new export orders had been placed.<ref name=trade>{{cite web |url=http://armstrade.sipri.org/armstrade/page/trade_register.php |title=Trade Registers |publisher=Armstrade.sipri.org |access-date=2013-06-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513073842/http://armstrade.sipri.org/armstrade/page/trade_register.php |archive-date=2011-05-13 |url-status=live }}</ref> Export of the Ratel only resumed again in the early 2000s, when the SANDF declared hundreds of its own IFVs surplus to requirements and offered them for sale.<ref name=Surplus/> The chief recipient of these vehicles was the [[Royal Jordanian Army]], which ordered 100 in 2002 and subsequently, another 221 in 2004.<ref name=trade/> The Jordanian government worked closely with a number of South African contractors, such as the Mechanology Design Bureau and [[Paramount Group]], to maintain and refurbish its Ratel fleet.<ref name="Jordan1">''[https://books.google.com/books?id=VFs-AQAAIAAJ Mechanology develops reconfigured Ratel infantry vehicle]''. Jane's International Defence Review, Volume 39. Jane's Information Group, 2006. p. 42.</ref> Some Jordanian Ratel-20s have been retrofitted with a new Cummins QSM11-C330 diesel engine developing 329&nbsp;hp (246&nbsp;kW).<ref name="Jordan1"/> This improved mechanical performance and extended the Ratels' maximum road speed to 110&nbsp;km/h.<ref name="Jordan1"/> The new engine necessitated a relocated engine compartment in the centre of the hull.<ref name="Jordan1"/>

A number of Jordanian Ratels were retrofitted with a BAU-23 turret carrying twin 23&nbsp;mm autocannon.<ref name="Security">{{cite web|title=Jordan|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://www.inss.org.il/he/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/systemfiles/Jordan20160103.pdf|location=Tel-Aviv
|publisher=Institute For National Security Studies|date=1 March 2016|access-date=12 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314022118/http://www.inss.org.il/he/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/systemfiles/Jordan20160103.pdf|archive-date=14 March 2018}}</ref> Others may have also been retrofitted with a turret carrying both the original 20&nbsp;mm autocannon in addition to a bank of ZT3 Ingwe missiles.<ref name="Defencemobile">{{cite web|title=Mobile Operations: Made in South Africa|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://www.defense-aerospace.com/articles-view/release/3/12340/denel-markets-strike-force-expertise-%28oct.-22%29.html|location=Neuilly Sur Seine, France|publisher=Briganti et Associés|date=21 October 2002|access-date=13 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314022459/http://www.defense-aerospace.com/articles-view/release/3/12340/denel-markets-strike-force-expertise-(oct.-22).html|archive-date=14 March 2018}}</ref> In addition to service with the Royal Jordanian Army, these modified Ratels were exported in small numbers to [[Yemen]] between 2008 and 2011.<ref name="Yemen1">{{cite news|title=Radebe fails to explain export of Jordanian Ratels to Yemen|last=Hartley|first=Wyndham|url=https://ww1.gcis.gov.za/spe/DownloadFileAction?id=154490&rnd=%7Brnd%7D|work=The Citizen|location=Johannesburg|date=15 November 2011|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318202652/https://ww1.gcis.gov.za/spe/DownloadFileAction?id=154490&rnd=%7Brnd%7D |archive-date=18 March 2018}}</ref> In Yemeni service, the Ratel was utilised for [[reconnaissance]] purposes and essentially fulfilled the role of an armoured car.<ref name="IISS2016"/> During the [[Yemeni Revolution]], photographs of Ratels seized by defecting army personnel were circulated in the international press, evoking considerable controversy.<ref name="Yemen1"/> The South African government acknowledged that it was notified of Jordan's intention to deliver the vehicles to Yemen, but had not formally consented to their transfer or amended the original [[end-user certificate|end-user agreement]], which made no provision for the re-export of Jordanian Ratels to third parties.<ref name="Yemen1"/> A similar controversy erupted when Ratels began appearing in [[Libya]]n service in 2013, prompting [[Democratic Alliance (South Africa)|Democratic Alliance]] defence spokesman [[David Maynier]] to call for a formal inquiry into how Libya could have acquired the vehicles without the knowledge of South Africa's National Conventional Arms Control Committee (NCACC).<ref name="Libya1">{{cite news|title=Why does Libya have Ratels, asks DA|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://www.iol.co.za/news/africa/why-does-libya-have-ratels-asks-da-1601768|work=IOL News|location=Cape Town|date=4 November 2013|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318205814/https://www.iol.co.za/news/africa/why-does-libya-have-ratels-asks-da-1601768 |archive-date=18 March 2018}}</ref> Maynier suggested that Libya, like Yemen, had likely obtained the Ratels from another country in violation of an end-user agreement.<ref name="Libya1"/> Ratels are currently operated by the [[Libyan National Army]],<ref name="Libya2">{{cite news|title=Islamists kidnap 25 Libyan soldiers, according to army|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://www.timesofmalta.com/articles/view/20140911/world/Islamists-kidnap-25-Libyan-soldiers-according-to-army.535261|work=Times of Malta|location=Valletta|date=11 September 2014|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141004165933/https://www.timesofmalta.com/articles/view/20140911/world/Islamists-kidnap-25-Libyan-soldiers-according-to-army.535261 |archive-date=4 October 2014}}</ref> as well as a number of unaffiliated militias such as the [[Zintan Brigades]] and the [[February 17th Martyrs Brigade]].<ref name="Libya3">{{cite web|title=Armed Groups in Libya After The Elections: What Can Be Expected?|last=Pusztai|first=Wolfgang|url=http://www.ispionline.it/sites/default/files/pubblicazioni/commentary_pusztai_25.06.2014.pdf|location=Milan|publisher=[[Institute for International Political Studies]]|date=25 June 2014|access-date=29 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180620231952/https://www.ispionline.it/sites/default/files/pubblicazioni/commentary_pusztai_25.06.2014.pdf|archive-date=20 June 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Military vehicles of the BIR in Far Northern Cameroon 2019.jpg|thumb|left|Ratels of the Rapid Intervention Battalion deployed in [[Far North Region, Cameroon|Far Northern Cameroon]] in January 2019.]]
Small quantities of second-hand Ratels have been delivered by the SANDF to a number of other African states, including [[Ghana]], which received 15 Ratel-20s and 24 Ratel-90s in 2004, and [[Rwanda]], which received 15 Ratel-90s and 20 Ratel-60s in 2007.<ref name=trade/> [[Senegal]] ordered 26 Ratel-20s in 2008 and had received them by 2010.<ref name=trade/> [[Zambia]] also received 20 refurbished ex-SANDF Ratel-20s in 2012.<ref name=trade/> [[Djibouti]] purchased 12 Ratel-90s in 2004 from an unknown source.<ref name=trade/> [[Cameroon]]'s [[Rapid Intervention Brigade]] acquired 12 Ratel-20s between 2015 and 2016 for [[demining]] operations in areas affected by the [[Boko Haram insurgency]].<ref name="CIED">{{cite web|title=Addressing the Threat Posed by IEDs: National, Regional, and Global Initiatives|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://ciedcoe.org/index.php/reports/analysis-reports/50-0003-addressing-the-threat-posed-by-ieds2017/file|location=London|publisher=Action On Armed Violence|date=2017|access-date=12 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314174542/https://ciedcoe.org/index.php/reports/analysis-reports/50-0003-addressing-the-threat-posed-by-ieds2017/file|archive-date=14 March 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2007, the SANDF committed to donate up to 18<ref name="IISS2016"/> Ratel-90s to the [[Central African Republic]] (CAR) under the auspices of [[South African military assistance to the Central African Republic|Operation Vimbezela]].<ref name="CAR1">{{cite news|title=Bozizé's frantic plea for weapons|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://mg.co.za/article/2013-04-06-00-bozize-in-frantic-plea-for-weapons|location=Johannesburg|work=[[Mail & Guardian]]|date=5 April 2013|access-date=29 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130408090207/https://mg.co.za/article/2013-04-06-00-bozize-in-frantic-plea-for-weapons|archive-date=8 April 2013}}</ref> This effort collapsed due to a variety of unforeseen problems: the SANDF was only willing to supply previously decommissioned Ratel-90s and insisted that the donation was contingent on the Central African government making its own arrangements to have them shipped to [[Bangui]].<ref name="CAR1"/> The latter possessed insufficient funds to restore all the Ratel-90s to serviceable condition or cover the shipping cost.<ref name="CAR1"/> Only 2 were delivered while the remainder were reclaimed by the South African contractor responsible for their refurbishment, citing unpaid shipping fees.<ref name="CAR1"/> Both Ratels arrived without adequate parts, maintenance equipment, or ammunition; nevertheless, they were utilised for training purposes by the SANDF mission in the CAR.<ref name="CAR2">{{cite book|last=Heitman|first=Helmoed-Römer|title=The Battle in Bangui: The Untold Story|date=2013|pages=9, 28–29|publisher=Parktown Publishers|location=Johannesburg|isbn=978-0-9921902-8-6}}</ref> At least three local crews were trained between 2010 and 2013,<ref name="Slides">{{cite web|title=Training Progress|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://pmg-assets.s3-website-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/170609VIMBEZELA_Part_2.pdf|location=Cape Town|publisher=South Africa Parliamentary Monitoring Group|date=2013|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319012254/http://pmg-assets.s3-website-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/170609VIMBEZELA_Part_2.pdf|archive-date=19 March 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> after which the vehicles were formally adopted by the [[Central African Armed Forces|Central African Army]].<ref name="CAR2"/> The Ratel-90s were deployed without success against [[Séléka]] militants during the country's [[Central African Republic Civil War (2012–2014)|2012–2014 civil war]].<ref name="CAR2"/> Their inexperienced crews failed to use them effectively in an offensive role,<ref name="CAR2"/> and ammunition shortages became so acute that President [[François Bozizé]] made personal appeals to South African officials for additional stocks of 90&nbsp;mm shells.<ref name="CAR1"/> After the end of the civil war, it was not clear whether the army retained the Ratel-90s or if either was operational.<ref name="IISS2016"/> An arms control panel appointed by the UN Security Council reported that they were still in the CAR in July 2014.<ref name="UN">{{cite web|title=Report of the Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic established pursuant to Security Council resolution 2127 (2013)|last1=Llorca|first1=Aurélien|last2=Handy|first2=Paul-Simon|last3=Himmiche|first3=Ahmed|last4=De Koning|first4=Ruben|last5=Reyes Aragón|first5=Carolina|url=https://reliefweb.int/sites/reliefweb.int/files/resources/N1441518.pdf|location=New York
|publisher=United Nations|date=26 July 2014|access-date=4 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170329063501/https://reliefweb.int/sites/reliefweb.int/files/resources/N1441518.pdf|archive-date=29 March 2017}}</ref>

The SANDF has also donated Ratels to multinational peacekeeping forces, namely the [[United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo]] (MONUSCO).<ref name=Hosken>{{cite web|url=https://www.iol.co.za/news/africa/sa-soldiers-in-heavy-drc-battles-422706 |title=SA soldiers in heavy DRC battles |publisher=South African Associated Press |date=2008-11-01 |access-date=2018-03-13 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314030548/https://www.iol.co.za/news/africa/sa-soldiers-in-heavy-drc-battles-422706 |archive-date=2018-03-14}}</ref>

== Description ==
The Ratel was based on a commercial [[MAN Truck & Bus|MAN]] truck chassis, from which many mechanical parts were utilised.<ref name=Harmse/> Its use of parts otherwise ubiquitous to the civilian automotive industry proved to be an advantage in circumventing the universal arms embargo imposed on South Africa, which extended only to purpose-built military products.<ref name="Henk">{{cite book | first = Daniel | last = Henk| title = South Africa's armaments industry: continuity and change after a decade of majority rule| year = 2006|edition= 2006|page= 164 | publisher = University Press America| isbn= 978-0761834823}}</ref> The vehicle is not amphibious and is not fitted with an [[CBRN defense|NBC]] overpressure system.<ref name="Forecast">{{cite web|title=Ratel|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=https://www.forecastinternational.com/archive/disp_old_pdf.cfm?ARC_ID=1166|location=Newtown, Connecticut, United States
|publisher=Forecast International, Incorporated|date=March 2003|access-date=29 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318022221/https://www.forecastinternational.com/archive/disp_old_pdf.cfm?ARC_ID=1166|archive-date=18 March 2018}}</ref> Most production model Ratels did not have any specialised night vision equipment.<ref name="Forecast"/> As an interim measure, the SADF occasionally issued Ratel crews with night vision goggles, which aided navigation in the Angolan bush where the use of headlamps was precluded due to proximity to enemy positions.<ref name="Mannall">{{cite book | first = David | last = Mannall| title = Battle on the Lomba 1987: The Day a South African Armoured Battalion shattered Angola's Last Mechanized Offensive| date = 19 November 2014|edition= 2014|page=182 | publisher = Helion and Company| isbn= 978-1-909982-02-4}}</ref> This was impractical for night fighting as muzzle flashes could blind the crew and the bulky goggles hampered movement and reaction speed in the turret.<ref name="Mannall"/> In the 1990s, Denel Land Systems developed night sights which could be fitted on new Ratel-20 turrets or retrofitted on older turrets.<ref name="Denel">{{cite web|title=LCT-20mm – LIW Compact Turret|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|url=http://www.denel.co.za/Landsystems/LS_TurretsLCT20.pdf|location=Centurion
|publisher=[[Denel Land Systems]]|date=2004|access-date=20 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050903151002/http://www.denel.co.za/Landsystems/LS_TurretsLCT20.pdf|archive-date=3 September 2005}}</ref>
[[File:Seats inside the Ratel at the South African National Museum of Military History June 2026.jpg|thumb|left|Seats inside a retired Ratel-20]]

The Ratel possesses rear-mounted engine and fighting compartments, while its turret ring and driving compartment are located towards the front of the vehicle.<ref name="Forecast"/> It has a long, box-shaped hull with slightly sloped vertical sides and rear.<ref name="Recognition"/> The hull is of all-welded construction, with a maximum armour thickness of 20&nbsp;mm on the hull front.<ref name="Recognition"/> Each Ratel hull is protected against [[7.62×39mm]] armour-piercing ammunition at any angle; it is also capable of stopping [[12.7×108mm]] armour-piercing ammunition on the frontal arc.<ref name="Forecast"/> The bottom of the hull structure is blastproof and vee-shaped to deflect mine explosions away from the passengers and crew.<ref name="Borderstrike"/> Ratels frequently detonated stacked anti-tank mines during the South African Border War with little injury to their occupants and minimal drive train damage.<ref name=SurviveRide/> On many occasions they were able to keep moving after basic field repairs.<ref name=SurviveRide/> Anti-tank mines common in Angola, such as the [[TMA-3 mine|TMA-3]], could destroy a Ratel's axles and occasionally damage its gearbox, but almost never penetrated its hull.<ref name=SurviveRide/>

The Ratel's crew consists of a section commander, driver, turret gunner, and rear gunner.<ref name="Forecast"/> In addition to the crew, an attached infantry section of nine is carried in the fighting compartment of the vehicle.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> There are three firing ports with vision blocks on either side of the fighting compartment.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> Passenger capacity may be reduced to six or seven if additional ammunition racks or radio equipment is carried.<ref name="Recognition"/><ref name=SurviveRide/> The infantry section debarks from three large, pneumatically sealed doors on either side of the hull and at the rear; it is also provided with five forward access hatches on the hull roof.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/>

The driver is seated at the front centre of the Ratel and provided with three bulletproof windscreens for use in a combat environment.<ref name="Forecast"/> This design feature was adopted directly from the [[Berliet VXB-170]] and favoured for its enhanced situational awareness.<ref name=Mobility/> The windscreens are fitted with armoured shutters which could be closed down as needed.<ref name="Forecast"/> Three vision periscopes are provided for the driver.<ref name="Forecast"/> The Ratel's steering system is mechanical, with hydraulic assistance.<ref name="Forecast"/> 
[[File:Ratel pintle MG.JPG|thumb|250px|One of the unique features of the Ratel's design was the pintle-mounted machine gun at the hull rear, which was used for anti-aircraft purposes by the vehicle crew.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/>]]
Ratel turrets are located towards the front of the vehicle, directly behind the driving compartment, and house two crew members: the section commander to the left and the turret gunner to the right.<ref name="Recognition"/><ref name="Forecast"/> Both crew members are provided with roof hatches; the commander is also afforded a domed cupola with vision blocks.<ref name="Forecast"/> The commander and gunner have nine day periscopes for all-round observation.<ref name="Forecast"/> The Ratel's standard armament is a [[20 mm modèle F2 gun|20 mm F2 M693]] automatic cannon<ref name=SurviveRide/> manufactured under licence as the [[Denel Land Systems GI-2|Denel GI-2]].<ref name=Harmse/> The autocannon may be elevated to a maximum of +38° for use against low-flying, fixed wing aircraft and helicopters.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> It has a selector switch used to alternate between three rates of fire&mdash;semi-automatic, limited burst, or fully automatic&mdash;and is belt fed from two ammunition chutes in the turret.<ref name="Pretty">{{cite book | last = Pretty| first = Ronald|title = Jane's Weapon Systems, 1979–80| year = 1980|edition= 1979|pages= 312–731 | publisher = Macdonald and Jane's Publishers Ltd| isbn= 978-0-531-03299-2}}</ref> The dual-feed system allows the gunner to swap between different projectile types fed from either chute as needed.<ref name=Harmse/><ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> Two types of ammunition can be selected: a high-explosive (HE) round with a range of 2,000 metres, or an armour-piercing tungsten carbide (APTC) round with a range of 1,000 metres.<ref name=SurviveRide/><ref name=Harmse/> The HE rounds have a muzzle velocity of 1,050&nbsp;m/s, while the armour-piercing round has an initial muzzle velocity of 1,300&nbsp;m/s and penetration of 20mm of [[rolled homogeneous armour]] at an incidence of 60°.<ref name="Pretty"/>

The GI-2 can achieve a cyclic rate of fire of 700 to 750 rounds per minute and 1,200 rounds of 20&nbsp;mm ammunition are carried on board.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> It provides the Ratel with a close support and anti-armour capability which proved sufficient to engage Angolan [[BTR-60]] APCs and light armoured cars such as the [[BRDM-2]] at long range.<ref name=Harmse/> While the autocannon is generally impotent against heavier armour, well-directed fire or exceptional shots are capable of damaging a tank's external features, especially its sights.<ref name="Scholtz"/> During Operation Moduler, one Ratel commander directed a stream of 20&nbsp;mm APTC rounds at an Angolan T-55 at close range, which apparently penetrated a vulnerable margin in its armour and caused a [[catastrophic kill]] after igniting the on-board ammunition.<ref name="Scholtz"/>

A co-axial 7.62&nbsp;mm [[Browning M1919]] machine gun is mounted to the left of the main armament on nearly all variants of the Ratel.<ref name="Forecast"/> Aside from the co-axial machine gun, a second 7.62&nbsp;mm Browning M1919 is carried at the rear of the vehicle's hull for anti-aircraft purposes.<ref name="Forecast"/> Both the Ratel-60 and Ratel-90 are also armed with a third 7.62&nbsp;mm M1919 on their turret roofs.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/> A maximum of 6,000 rounds of 7.62&nbsp;mm ammunition are carried within the vehicle.<ref name="HeitmanSAA"/>

The Ratel is powered by a six-cylinder, liquid-cooled, turbocharged D 3256 BTXF diesel engine.<ref name="Forecast"/> This is housed in an engine compartment at the rear left of the hull and coupled to a fully automatic RENK HSU 106 automatic gearbox with six forward and two reverse gear ratios.<ref name="Forecast"/> The gearbox can be operated manually and has a mechanical emergency gearshift.<ref name=SurviveRide/> Drive is transmitted to the Ratel's three axles in two stages, with final reduction being achieved by epicyclic gearing in the wheel hubs.<ref name=SurviveRide/> The three axles have their own locking differentials and longitudinal differential locks.<ref name=SurviveRide/> There are hydropneumatic shock dampers at each wheel station.<ref name="Forecast"/>
